title: Editing with Generative Fill and Expand

production_notes: [VERSION] Record the screen demo only after checking the live tool: Adobe Firefly feature names (Generative Fill, Generative Expand), the remove and insert brushes, button labels, the aspect-ratio menu, whether the expand prompt can be left empty, and free-tier generative credits all change often. Update the screen_steps if menu names differ.
The square workshop image is generated by the team in advance in Gemini or Firefly, with a plastic bottle on the left of the counter. No people, logos or readable brand names on tools or products.
Scene 13 (edge check): if the recorded expansion shows no repeated tools or bent lines, the presenter says the edges look clean and keeps the reason for checking.
Use a demo Adobe account with no personal data visible. Blur account names, email addresses and credit balances.
Nino and her Tbilisi bicycle repair shop are fictional.

Hook.voiceover: You have an almost perfect image. But there is a coffee cup in the corner that should not be there, and the image is square when your website needs a wide banner. Do you start again? No. You edit only the part that needs to change.

Explain.voiceover: Two editing features save a great deal of time. The first is generative fill. It changes a selected area of an image.

slide.title: Editing with Generative Fill and Expand
slide.body: AI Image Generation and Visual Design · Lesson 7 of 12 · Screen demo. Two icons: a brush over a selection (Fill) and a frame growing outwards (Expand).

Explain.voiceover: You paint over part of the picture. This is called a selection, or a mask. Then you can remove what is there, and the tool fills the space with matching background. Or you can write a short prompt, like a green potted plant, and the tool creates it only inside the selection. This is also called inpainting.

slide.title: Generative fill = inpainting
slide.body: An image with a painted selection. Two arrows: Remove → space filled with matching background · Add or replace → short prompt 'a green potted plant' creates it inside the selection. Label: everything outside the selection stays the same.

Explain.voiceover: The second is generative expand, also called outpainting. It makes the canvas larger and fills the new space so that it continues the original image. It is the best way to turn a square image into a wide banner or a tall story, without stretching or cutting the subject.

slide.title: Generative expand = outpainting
slide.body: A square image in the centre of a wider 16:9 frame and a taller 9:16 frame; the new areas are shaded and labelled 'continues the scene'. Crossed-out small example of a stretched image.

Explain.voiceover: In Adobe Firefly, these features have names like Generative Fill and Generative Expand. They use generative credits, and the free tier has a limit. Three tips. Select a little more than the object, including its shadow. Keep fill prompts short and concrete. And after a big expansion, check the new edges carefully.

slide.title: Tips for good results
slide.body: Select a little more than the object, including its shadow · Short, concrete fill prompts: 'empty wooden shelf' · Big expansions can repeat details: check the edges · Each edit uses generative credits

Explain.voiceover: Generative fill is like a skilled painter who repairs one damaged patch of wall, so well that you cannot see the repair. Generative expand is like adding a new section to a mural, painted to continue the scene.
One safety note. Only edit images you have the right to use, and do not upload photos of people without their consent.
Explain.on_screen_text: Edit only images you may use

Demonstrate.voiceover: Let's help Nino. She owns a bicycle repair shop in Tbilisi, Georgia. She has a square AI image of her workshop counter. But there is a plastic bottle on the left that looks untidy, and her website needs a wide banner.

slide.title: Nino's workshop image
slide.body: Left: the square generated workshop counter with the plastic bottle circled. Right: an empty 16:9 website banner outline with 'headline goes here' on the left.

Demonstrate.voiceover: I open Adobe Firefly, choose Generative Fill and upload the square image. I choose the remove brush and paint over the bottle, and its shadow too.
screen_steps: Open Adobe Firefly and sign in
Choose the Generative Fill option and upload the square workshop image
Choose the remove tool or brush
Paint over the bottle and its shadow
Demonstrate.on_screen_text: Select the object and its shadow

Demonstrate.voiceover: I click remove. The tool offers a few results. I compare them, choose the one with the cleanest counter surface, and keep it.
screen_steps: Click the remove or generate button
Compare the results offered
Choose the one with the cleanest counter surface and keep it

Demonstrate.voiceover: Now let's add something. With the insert brush, I select a small empty area on the right of the counter. I type a short prompt, a small green potted plant in a metal pot, and generate. I choose the result that matches the light direction of the image.
screen_steps: Choose the insert or add brush
Select a small empty area on the right of the counter
Type: 'a small green potted plant in a metal pot'
Click Generate
Choose the result that matches the light direction

Demonstrate.voiceover: Next, the banner. I open Generative Expand with the edited image and choose sixteen by nine from the ratio menu. I move the original image to the right, so the new empty area appears on the left, where the headline will go.
screen_steps: Open the Generative Expand option with the edited image
Choose the 16:9 aspect ratio from the size or ratio menu
Move the original image to the right inside the new frame, leaving space on the left

Demonstrate.voiceover: I can leave the prompt empty so the tool continues the scene, or add plain workshop wall for a calmer background. I generate, then check the new edges for repeated tools or bent lines, and download the best result.
screen_steps: Leave the prompt empty, or type 'plain workshop wall'
Click Generate
Zoom in on the new edges and check for repeated tools or bent lines
Download the best result

Demonstrate.voiceover: Here is the final banner. Nino's tidy counter is on the right, and a quiet wall is on the left, ready for text in Canva.
screen_steps: Show the square original and the final 16:9 banner side by side
Point to the empty wall on the left, ready for a headline

Demonstrate.voiceover: A common mistake is to select only the object, not its shadow. The object disappears, but a shadow of nothing remains. Another mistake is to regenerate the whole image for one small problem. That wastes credits and can lose the parts you liked. Edit the area first.

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, generative fill, or inpainting, removes, adds or replaces objects inside a selected area, and keeps the rest of the image the same. Second, generative expand, or outpainting, extends the canvas to a new shape, like square to sixteen by nine, without stretching the subject. Third, select objects with their shadows, keep fill prompts short, and check new edges carefully.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Fill (inpainting): change only the selected area. 2. Expand (outpainting): new aspect ratio, no stretching. 3. Select shadows too, keep prompts short, check edges.

CTA.voiceover: Now it is your turn. In the exercise below, you will take one of your own square images, remove an unwanted object in Firefly, and expand it to sixteen by nine. It takes about twenty minutes. In the next lesson, we finish in Canva, with layouts, resizing and text. See you there.
